transcript:
Meeting header: 2027-09-30 15:30 UTC | Duration: ~52m | Recording: on
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam Park (Redwood SE), Sofia Martinez (Peregrine Head of ML), Rajesh Patel (Infra), Emily Rivers (CTO), Tommy Lo (SRE)

Summary: quick alignment on dedicated reserved GPU requirements, isolation needs, burst strategy for seasonal spikes, and security constraints for a Private/VPC option. Customer wants cost/latency tradeoffs and a concrete prewarm/burst playbook.

Topics: reserved GPUs, tenant isolation, hot pool / prewarm, failover to hosted fallback, VPC/KMS, benchmarking, SLA, timeline for pilot.

00:00 Maya Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh, we'll keep this focused. I'm Maya, AE for Redwood inference. Liam's our SE who'll dig into ops and topology. Can folks intro quickly?
00:12 Sofia Martinez: yeah hi I'm Sofia, head of ML at Peregrine. We're evaluating options for moving our realtime scoring to a dedicated infra, mostly to control costs and meet residency and audit needs.
00:19 Emily Rivers: Emily here, CTO, focusing on compliance and operational ownership.
00:24 Rajesh Patel: Rajesh, infra -- I own the cluster provisioning and network side. Tommy's covering SRE.
00:29 Tommy Lo: hey.
00:32 Liam Park: cool, thanks. quick framing — curious about current traffic patterns and burst characteristics. Sofia, can you sketch typical RPS, tails, and any synchronized events?
00:44 Sofia Martinez: sure. so baseline is 30 RPS for our inference endpoint, spikes to 600 RPS for a few minutes during ingest windows — it's predictable, happens 2–3 times a day. We also have a weekly marketing campaign that can blow up to 2k RPS for 20–30 minutes. Latency target is 150ms p95, 350ms p99. We're currently on a managed cloud endpoint with high unit costs.
01:05 Liam Park: got it. so three tiers of load — baseline, short predictable spikes, and less frequent big bursts. For Dedicated, are you looking for reserved GPUs with burst buffers / warm pool or a pure dedicated pool with autoscale?
01:20 Sofia Martinez: we'd prefer reserved for predictability, but we need isolation between customers in multi-tenant parts of the app. Also private deployment inside our VPC is a must for now.
01:30 Emily Rivers: and encryption keys must be customer-managed, KMS / HSM. SOC2 and audit logs are non-negotiable.
01:36 Maya Chen: that's all supported — Redwood Private offers VPC deployment, KMS integrations, audit logging. We'll share the SOC 2 pack and the private runbook after.
01:44 Rajesh Patel: quick question on isolation — we run some third-party analytics (multi-tenant) workloads on same cluster. We need hard tenant fencing during surge so noisy neighbors don't evict critical models. What isolation options exist?
01:56 Liam Park: two primary patterns we recommend: 1) reserved Dedicated node pools per tenant/service for hard isolation — physical or instance-level isolation, no overcommit; 2) warm-pool hybrid where you maintain a hot pool for low-latency shared models with strict cgroups and QoS and preemption policies. For strict compliance you'd go reserved nodes. For cost-efficiency we can suggest soft-isolation with tenant quotas + throttling.
02:20 Sofia Martinez: okay, reserved nodes likely for our core models. But for research workloads, we can do soft. How about burst? if we reserve for baseline, what's cost to handle the 2k RPS campaign?
02:33 Liam Park: costwise, there are two levers — prewarm (pay for GPU time even when idle) and on-demand burst into a warm shared pool which may be slightly higher latency. We can model the 2k RPS event as short-lived prewarm windows: prewarm X GPUs 30 minutes before campaign. Alternatively, set up a bursting policy to Redwood Hosted fallback for excess traffic — that avoids prewarm costs but introduces egress/data residency considerations.
02:55 Emily Rivers: fallback to hosted is risky for us because of data residency. We might be able to sanitize or route non-PII to hosted, but ideally we keep everything inside VPC or on-prem.
03:05 Tommy Lo: also we don't want to pay for prewarm 24/7. Can Redwood ramp GPUs in 2–3 minutes?
03:13 Liam Park: warmup times depend on instance spin-up and model load. With Dedicated reserved pools we recommend keeping a small hot pool for immediate spikes — think 10–20% of expected burst capability — and use autoscale to add nodes for the remainder. In our benchmarks, cold-start plus model load for 70B-ish models can be 2–6 minutes; for smaller models it's sub-90s. We also have snapshot-backed rapid boot paths and checkpoint loaders to reduce time; we'll include the numbers in the cost sheet.
03:40 Sofia Martinez: can you quantify warm-pool sizing? like if our target for campaign is 2k RPS and baseline 30 RPS, what's the hot pool?
03:49 Liam Park: rough rule: hot-pool to cover your p95 latency for the first 90s of spike. if your average token throughput per request is low, a handful of A10/30-ish GPUs can cover small bursts; for your 2k RPS, likely need dozens. We'll model using your exact payload sizes.
04:05 Rajesh Patel: another operational question — how does tenant fencing work under node failure? if a reserved node goes down, do models failover to a shared pool and potentially cross-tenant?
04:15 Liam Park: good question. failover is configurable. We recommend policy options: strict-failfast (reject beyond capacity) or degrade-to-shared-fallback (fails over into a protected shared pool that still enforces RBAC but may have different latency). For strict compliance choose strict-failfast plus standby reserved nodes. We can also set up prioritized preemption so critical tenants pop back in.
04:37 Emily Rivers: what's the small print on SLAs for Dedicated?
04:40 Maya Chen: Dedicated comes with an SLA for node availability — we'll attach the latest SLA PDF. For latency SLOs we provide observability and can support contractual latency SLAs with appropriate capacity commitments.
04:48 Sofia Martinez: operationally, who owns the orchestration in Private VPC? us or Redwood?
04:53 Maya Chen: for Redwood Private we run a control plane but the compute plane can be customer-managed. There are two variants: 1) control plane hosted by Redwood but connected via VPC peering, we orchestrate/monitor; 2) fully on-prem where you host both plane and compute — that's more hands-on. We'll map those options in the runbook.
05:10 Tommy Lo: curious about key management — can we bring our own HSM?
05:13 Liam Park: yes, we integrate with customer KMS/HSM for key wrapping; you'll keep your KMS in your cloud account. We'll document supported providers.
05:21 Sofia Martinez: on the model side, do you support mixed-quant and lower precision to reduce GPU memory and increase density?
05:26 Liam Park: yes, runtime supports int8/4 quantization and kernel selection. We can host different quantized variants and do routing by policy for latency vs cost. Also model pinning for rollouts and canary.
05:36 Rajesh Patel: what about autoscaling policy details — how predictable is autoscale under noisy workloads? we saw some autoscalers behave badly on short spikes.
05:44 Liam Park: Redwood uses request-based metrics and custom smoothing with lookahead heuristics; you can set min/max nodes, scale steps, and warm-pool thresholds. For your pattern (very short but big spikes) autoscale alone is insufficient; combine warm pool plus autoscale and optional prewarm windows driven by scheduled events or market signals.
06:05 Sofia Martinez: okay makes sense. For approval, Emily needs a cost estimate and a security posture doc.
06:11 Maya Chen: we'll send SOC2, private runbook, and a cost workbook. Liam will do two topology proposals: strict-reserved for core models, hybrid for research.
06:20 Emily Rivers: timeline — we want a pilot in Q4, ideally mid-late Oct. Can you support a 4-week pilot with two reserved nodes and a warm pool?
06:28 Liam Park: yes, pilots are common. We'll specify the pilot scope in the follow-up.
06:32 Sofia Martinez: one more — do you provide per-route token billing or is it per-request? we need cost breakdown by route and model.
06:39 Maya Chen: per-token for generative; for inference we can do per-request or custom meter depending on Dedicated contract. Console has token-level and route breakdowns.
06:47 Rajesh Patel: network egress costs — if fallback to hosted is used, what about VPC egress and throughput caps?
06:54 Liam Park: that'll be documented; egress costs are customer account dependent; we'll show two architectures: full VPC-only with no egress to hosted vs hybrid.
07:02 Tommy Lo: are you able to run a small benchmark with our sample payload to reproduce p95/p99 on dedicated nodes?
07:07 Liam Park: yes, please send a small sample dataset and a synthetic load file; we can run an internal perf test and share the csv.
07:13 Sofia Martinez: noted, I'll send JSON payloads and traffic profile.
07:17 Maya Chen: recap / next steps — Liam to produce topology + burst cost sheet by Oct 6; Maya to send SOC2 + Private runbook by Oct 4; Peregrine to send sample payloads and RPS profile by Oct 5; schedule pilot kickoff week of Oct 18. Does that match?
07:30 Emily Rivers: yes.
07:32 Sofia Martinez: yes, thanks.
07:34 Maya Chen: excellent, we'll follow up with links: SOC2 pack, dedicated runbook, tenancy playbook (e.g., https://redwood.example.com/tenancy-playbook) and the cost template link (https://redwood.example.com/pilot-costs).
07:46 Liam Park: quick note — I'll include two failure scenarios in the doc: node loss with strict failfast and node loss with shared fallback, plus estimated cost impact.
07:55 Sofia Martinez: cool. thanks everyone.

Meeting end.
